detailed_rationale:
Aegis Logistics is one of India's largest independent energy logistics platforms -- bulk liquid terminals, LPG import/storage/distribution and gas stations -- and its recent numbers show the capex cycle finally converting to earnings. Q4 FY26 (Mar 2026) revenue was Rs 2,594 Cr with net profit of Rs 455 Cr (24% margin), capping full-year FY26 sales of Rs 8,333 Cr and net profit of Rs 1,107 Cr (EPS Rs 25.59), with a 34% dividend payout and a final dividend of Rs 6.70/share recommended. ROE has held a consistent ~16% and ROCE ~13-15% over multiple years, evidence this is a real, functioning logistics franchise rather than a story stock.

The reason it is not a rescue-to-something-stronger name is the balance sheet trajectory: borrowings have climbed from Rs 2,665 Cr (Mar 2024) to Rs 4,150 Cr (Mar 2026) as the company (through the Aegis Vopak Terminals JV) builds out cryogenic LPG and chemical terminal capacity -- a legitimate growth capex program, but one that raises leverage risk if utilization ramps slower than planned. We also flag, as a genuine earnings-quality watch item rather than a confirmed problem, a note that the company may be capitalizing interest cost on this capex program -- if so, reported margins are flattered versus a scenario where that interest hit the P&L directly; we could not verify the exact accounting treatment from the sources available and are not treating this as more than a 'watch.'

At a live PE near 50-56x, Aegis is priced as a structural growth story (India's LPG/gas logistics build-out, energy security, C&I fuel-switching), and the recent quarters' revenue and profit growth support that narrative. But the multiple already assumes the new capacity gets utilized profitably; if the Vopak JV ramp disappoints, both the earnings growth and the multiple compress together.
recommendation_rationale: Hold, matching the quant score -- genuine, profitable growth and a real logistics franchise argue against a Sell, but rising leverage funding still-ramping capacity plus a rich multiple and an unverified interest-capitalization flag argue against treating this as anything more enthusiastic than a Hold.
summary: Aegis Logistics runs India's LPG and bulk-liquid energy logistics infrastructure, and its FY26 numbers show strong, profitable growth (revenue Rs 8,333 Cr, profit Rs 1,107 Cr, steady ~16% ROE) as new import/storage capacity comes online through its Vopak joint venture. Debt has risen meaningfully to fund that capacity build-out, and the stock's valuation already prices in continued success of that expansion. We rate it a Hold: a genuine growth business, but priced for that growth to keep showing up on schedule.
positive_para: Aegis has a real, moaty position in Indian energy logistics (LPG import/storage/distribution plus bulk liquid terminals), consistent ~16% ROE over multiple years, and profitable, accelerating growth as new Vopak JV capacity comes online (Q4 FY26 profit +43% YoY). The business benefits from structural tailwinds in Indian gas/LPG consumption and energy security policy.
negative_para: Borrowings have grown roughly 55% in two years to fund capacity still being commissioned, and a screener-flagged possibility that interest cost is being capitalized (rather than expensed) means reported margins could be somewhat flattered versus the cash economics -- we could not confirm or rule this out from the sources available, so it stays a watch item, not a settled finding. At a 50x-plus multiple, the market is already paying up for the JV ramp to go right; any slippage in utilization or a rate environment that makes the added debt costlier would compress both earnings growth and the multiple at the same time.
reverse_dcf_judgment: At a ~50-56x multiple, the market is pricing several more years of the Vopak JV capacity ramping to full utilization at healthy margins. The historical ~16% ROE and real infrastructure moat support paying up somewhat, but the multiple leaves little cushion if commissioning is delayed or if the (unverified) interest-capitalization practice means true cash returns on the new capex are lower than reported margins suggest. Fair-to-rich, contingent on flawless execution of a large capex program.
